transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-27 15:00 UTC | Duration: 45m | Recording: yes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jared (Redwood SE), Anton (Redwood SE), Elena (Head of ML - Stellarex), Tom (CTO), Priya (Infra), Aaron (SRE)

Auto-summary (auto-generated): short walkthrough of Redwood Optimize focusing on batching and KV/prefix cache, cost model examples for payments use case; next steps and action items captured.

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh it's Maya from Redwood, I'm the AE on this account. Jared's gonna walk through the Optimize recommendations — batching, KV cache, cost modeling — and we'll flag tradeoffs for latency vs cost.
[00:20] Tom: Yep thanks, quick call, we wanna see concrete numbers. P95 matters for our checkout flow.
[00:30] Jared: Great, quick agenda: 1) explain continuous batching behavior and the impact on P95, 2) prefix vs KV cache — when to use each, 3) cost model with some sample numbers, and 4) pilot plan. Sound good?
[00:45] Elena: Yep, please; and we have some concerns around PCI scope and data residency — we'll raise those as we go.
[01:10] Jared: Totally. Ok starting with batching — so Redwood's runtime does continuous batching. That means short windows where we accumulate requests to improve GPU utilization, but we enforce latency SLOs via per-route targets. For example in our benchmarks, at 200 req/s with an average prompt length of 150 tokens, enabling small batch size growth dropped cost per token ~18% while increasing P95 from 110ms to 170ms.
[02:05] Priya: Can you clarify 'batch size growth'? Like is that auto or configured?
[02:12] Jared: It's a mix — we have an autoscaling batching policy, but you can pin a max batch size per model/route. For latency-critical routes you pin lower batch max. For background scoring you allow larger maximums.
[02:40] Anton: Also worth noting the kernel selection and quantization we run picks the most compact FP16/INT8 paths which affects per-token throughput. So batching wins multiply with quantization.
[03:05] Elena: Ok, good — show us prefix vs KV cache, we weren't 100% on those.
[03:12] Jared: Sure. Prefix caching keeps the initial prompt prefixes in memory and reuses them to avoid recomputing early layers. It's cheap and great for systems where the majority of tokens are shared prefixes — e.g., internal system messages, policy text, or repeated UI scaffolding. KV cache (key-value cache) stores per-session KV states of the transformer to skip computing attention for past tokens — much more effective for multi-turn chat or long context retrieval.
[04:00] Tom: Which one reduces cost more for long-lived sessions?
[04:05] Jared: KV cache usually has larger wins for long interactions because each token saved avoids full attention recompute; but KV cache has memory and warm-up implications. For a payments chatbot with 6-turn average, KV can cut token compute by ~40-60% depending on turn lengths.
[04:45] Aaron: Are there evictions? How do we size the KV cache?
[04:50] Jared: Yes, cache eviction follows an LRU policy and you can tune TTL and per-session limits. Redwood Optimize recommends sizing based on 95th percentile session length; we provide a sizing guide and a simulation tool — the cost model uses that to estimate memory footprint and hit rates.
[05:30] Elena: Can you show a concrete cost table — like per-transaction numbers if we use hosted vs dedicated?
[05:38] Jared: Yep pulling up a sample. (brief pause) Ok example: baseline: hosted API, no KV, small batching tuned for <120ms P95: cost ~ $0.0035 per tx. Dedicated with moderate batching + prefix cache: $0.0026 per tx. Dedicated with KV cache enabled and 80% hit rate: $0.0017 per tx. These are illustrative and assume the same model variant (7B quantized) and prompt/response lengths of 120/80 tokens.
[06:30] Tom: Those deltas are large — what's the tradeoff in latency?
[06:35] Jared: With KV enabled and larger batches P95 drifted up to 220-260ms in our bench, but average latency improved. For strict P95 SLAs we suggested a hybrid: critical route pinned to lower batch/max cache TTL so you get 130-180ms P95 while background routes use aggressive batching/KV caching.
[07:10] Priya: How does this interact with model variant selection — do you recommend quantized 7B or a larger 13B?
[07:20] Jared: Usually quantized 7B is best price/perf. 13B gives better quality but costs ~1.8x–2x. If you need quality uplift for certain prompts, Redwood supports model routing policies: route quality-sensitive prompts to 13B and everything else to 7B. Runtime does fast fallbacks if capacity constrained.
[07:55] Elena: On the security side — we need details about KMS and data encryption. Are requests stored for caching?
[08:05] Maya: Good Q. Cache entries (both prefix and KV) are stored in memory/GPU-local stores by default; optional persistent caching uses encrypted stores. For Private/VPC customers we can run cache within their network; for Hosted we encrypt at rest and in transit and support customer-managed KMS for keys. We'll share SOC2 docs and KMS integration guide after the call.
[08:40] Tom: Nice. Also curious about how we keep PCI out of scope — storing payment tokens in cache is a no-no.
[08:50] Jared: Exactly — we recommend redaction at ingress and not caching sensitive tokens. Redwood Optimize can apply automatic redaction rules and you can configure route-level cache exemptions.
[09:10] Elena: Back to cost model assumptions: what's a typical hit rate for KV cache in a payments flow?
[09:18] Jared: It varies — for 6–8 turn flows we see hit rates 55–80% depending on how repetitive user queries are and whether you use retrieval augmentation. If most tokens are dynamic (like amounts, IDs) hit rate drops. Our modeling tool runs permutations over your sample traces to estimate realistic hit rates.
[09:50] Aaron: If we wanted to run a pilot, what do you need from us?
[09:55] Maya: Sample request traces (anonymized), target success criteria (latency, quality thresholds), and expected daily QPS. Ideally a 2-week window of representative traffic.
[10:10] Priya: We can provide an anonymized trace and sample prompts; will do.
[10:20] Jared: Great. I'll also call out edge cases: small requests at high concurrency can defeat batching benefits because batch windows are short; conversely bursty traffic benefits more. Our advice is route-level configs per endpoint.
[11:00] Elena: Anything else on cost comps — do you factor in autoscaling overhead and reserved capacity?
[11:05] Jared: Yes. Dedicated reserved pools have a fixed monthly commit plus a lower per-token execution cost — in our cost model we amortize the GPU cost across expected throughput. If you have predictable traffic, reserved capacity plus intelligent batching often lowers total cost. For burst allowances Redwood provides burst capacity pricing too.
[11:40] Tom: Competitors we looked at (Anthropic/Vertex) do similar caching?
[11:45] Jared: Some do prefix caching, but KV cache integration at runtime level plus transparent cost modeling and rollouts is a differentiator. Self-hosted Triton setups require you to build caching and routing logic.
[12:05] Anton: Quick note on telemetry — Console shows token-level cost, cache hit rates, and per-route latency percentiles so you can tune configs iteratively.
[12:35] Elena: Ok -- can you show the spreadsheet numbers for our 1M daily tx sample?
[12:40] Jared: Sure, walking through an example: assumptions: 1M tx/day, avg prompt 120 tokens, response 80 tokens => total tokens 200 per tx => 200M tokens/day. Model cost baseline 7B quantized: $X per million tokens. If we apply KV with 60% hit rate we reduce compute tokens by ~60% of previous responses which gives net token count ~120M => cost reduction ~40%. With reserved dedicated and batching you further reduce. (Jared types / brief pause)
[13:40] Priya: Can you send that calc exported?
[13:45] Maya: We'll send the spreadsheet after the call.
[13:50] Elena: Are there any constraints around private deployments vs hosted for this pilot? We may need VPC isolation for the pilot dataset.
[13:58] Maya: We can run the initial pilot on Dedicated in our shared cloud with network isolation and then move to Private/VPC if you need on-prem or customer-managed network. For tight compliance we'd do Private.
[14:20] Aaron: For cache persistence — do you persist KV across restarts?
[14:25] Jared: By default KV cache is in-memory on the serving instance — it's ephemeral. You can enable warm caches or preloading strategies for stable sessions; persistent cache strategies are available for Private deployments.
[14:48] Tom: Any risk of cross-tenant leakage?
[14:52] Jared: No, caches are scoped per-customer/tenant; memory is partitioned, and for hosted we do extra isolation layers. We'll include architecture diagrams in the docs.
[15:20] (demo pause) Jared: Ok I'm switching to the Console view — here's per-route latency chart, token cost breakdown, cache hit-rate widget. You can drill into a route and see recommended batch sizes and expected P95 impact.
[16:05] Elena: That UI looks useful, can we set alerts if hit-rate drops or cache eviction spikes?
[16:10] Anton: Yup, you can set alerts on hit-rate, P95, and cost thresholds; we also have regression alerts tied to evals.
[16:30] Priya: On sampling: what format do you want traces in?
[16:34] Maya: CSV with columns: timestamp, route, prompt_length, response_length, session_id (anonymized), latency_ms — or JSONL with same fields. We'll attach a template.
[16:50] Aaron: We'll produce that by end of week.
[17:00] Elena: For success criteria we want P95 <= 250ms on checkout, with cost <= $0.002 per tx as a stretch goal.
[17:10] Maya: Noted. We'll model that. Jared, anything else to call out?
[17:16] Jared: One operational note — when using KV cache it's important to watch memory pressure and set TTLs; Optimize will flag routes where hit-rate gain doesn't justify memory cost. Also, retrieval-augmented prompts can increase hit-rate by normalizing retrieved content.
[17:40] Tom: Thank you — what's our timeline?
[17:44] Maya: If you provide traces by Tuesday (2026-03-31) we can kick off benchmark the same week and aim to have pilot results within 2 weeks.
[17:55] Elena: Sounds good.
[18:05] (wrap-up) Maya: Recap: Redwood to share pricing spreadsheet, pilot SOW, SOC2/KMS/VPC docs; SE to run cost model and pilot once we get traces; next call scheduled after pilot results.
[18:25] Tom: Great, thanks all.
[18:30] End of recording.
